I mentioned that on May 9,1 believe it was, the Leader of the Opposition got up. He had reviewed the government's leaked budget papers. He had seen something referred to as CPI minus 3. CPI minus 3 seems like an innocuous few letters and a number that does not quite mean very much. CPI minus 3 means an awful lot and should mean an awful lot to those working Canadians who are currently planning their retirement.
What CPI minus 3 means is that there will not be full indexing of the measures in Bill C-28. That is what it means. It means that it will be indexed to the inflation rate minus 3 per cent.
On May 9, the Leader of the Opposition asked the Minister of Finance: "What exactly does this mean? What does this mean to Canadians who are planning their retirement income now?"
I spoke about those senior citizens who will have clawed back and scratched back and gouged back some of their pension income that they expected to receive. Now I will talk about some of those other Canadians who are 35, 45, or 55 years of age and have to be concerned about
Government Orders
this particular piece of legislation. They should be concerned because of the CPI minus 3.
I am going to go back and quote a question from the Leader of the Opposition to the Minister of Finance on May 9, as reported at page 1492 of Hansard. Referring to the Minister of Finance he asked:
I want to use his formula which he cutely calls CPI minus 3. Using his formula, will the minister confirm that 55-year old Canadians whose incomes are currently $ 25,000 a year as a result of inflation will have their old age pensions taxed back at age 80?
That is a pretty serious flaw in this legislation. Nobody would ever expect that their government would be so cruel and callous to intentionally do that to them.
The answer from the Minister of Finance was all huff and puffery. He knew that the Leader of the Opposition had found out what he was trying to do. This provision, CPI minus 3, means that by the time people currently making $25,000 a year or is looking at a pension income of $25,000 a year at age 55 turns 80, they will have all of their old age security taxed back. The government plays a cute game. They use $50,000 like it is the end of the world, that if somebody makes $50,000 a year, they are wealthy, they are rich.
Yesterday, I and other members from this side blew apart that particular falsehood. If there is anybody out there still saying that $50,000 seems like a lot and is 55, then he should think about an income of $25,000. Anybody who looks at an actuarial table could tell us that Canadians are living longer. The average life span for males is something like 77 and for females it is 79, and it increases every year. We can reasonably expect, if one is 55 today, it is not far-fetched to talk about living well past the age of 80.
As a matter of fact, I read a recent article in a news magazine. It was an American article which talked about the growth of centenarians, those in our society who are over 100 years of age. This is the fastest growing age group in North America. By the year 2025, it was estimated in the article, there will be 1.6 million North Americans over the age of 100.
When people sit back and say "well, this bill is not going to affect me; I am 55 and 80 is a long way off", they should just think about trying to plan their retirement knowing that at age 80, when they are not capable of working or are in their retirement years by choice, the pension income they had come to expect has been taxed back because of the actions of this government in this Bill C-28 in December 1989. The negative effects of this

Government Orders
bill will ripple through the next 40 or 50 years, if the bill is not changed, is passed and any other Conservative government tries to keep the bill as law.
There was another thing the Leader of the Opposition asked that day. He put forth a second hypothetical scenario. Just so we know that we are not only dealing with 55-year-olds, 65-year-olds and 75-year olds, he asked the minister whether he would confirm that 45-year old Canadians whose incomes were $18,000 would as a result of the same formula have their old age pension taxed back at age 80. That is the fact. Taking into account the average rate of inflation over the last number of years, by the time somebody who makes $18,000 and is 45 years of age reaches 80 years of age, $18,000 will be the threshold.
I cannot think of another bill I have seen in this place that has had such a far-reaching impact on the future. The government does what it always does: It tries to hide the effects. It never comes forward and says: "Listen, we are going to end universality. We are going to try to get out of the old age pension system. We are going to tax everything back".
The government tries to put it in legalese language, to hide it with 57 or 58 other changes in the Income Tax Act and other related acts, and to hope that people on this side of the House will not do their homework and find out what is its true agenda. The people on this side of the House have done their homework. We know what is the government's true agenda. That is why we are vigorously opposing this particular piece of legislation.
Motions were put forward by my colleague from Ottawa South. The effect of Motion No. 4 would be to strike out in clause 48, lines 1 to 40, at page 46. In effect what this motion would do is destroy the clawback, the main intent of this bill and of this government's devious acts against those trying to plan their retirement income, not just those of today but those who will be retired in the future.
I am a realist. Unless my comments and the comments of the seniors and other concerned Canadians around the country have had an effect, I know the government will push forward with this piece of legislation to pull back what Canadians have a right to expect from their
government. That is why I rise today to support Motion No. 4 on behalf of my colleagues, on behalf of seniors, on behalf of working people in my riding, and on behalf of all other Canadians.

Madam Speaker, I would like to contribute to this debate on the report of the parliamentary committee which is involved in clause-by-clause consideration of Bill C-28, to remind my colleagues and especially the people watching, that this clawback measure is basically a progressive one. I am astonished that our friends opposite are trying to protect the rich. Essentially, this measure is aimed at the people who are best able to bear it and at making them help us put the country's finances back on track, while leaving the principle of universality intact.
The Canadian Council on Social Development said last year that the advantage of the clawback was that it was possible to achieve a saving while enhancing the progressive aspect of social programs and leaving the controversial principle of universality untouched. Most proponents of universality feel that benefits should be distributed progressively. The higher your income, the less you should receive and vice versa. The clawback does not jeopardize universality. Seniors and parents will continue to get their old age pension cheques and family allowances whatever their income, but the clawback reduces the net value for high-income beneficiaries.
I think that is very important. In practice, for those listening to us, it means people whose gross income is over $70,000.
I recently had the opportunity to visit seniors in my riding. I talked to them and was not afraid-we are accused of not being open. I am not afraid to talk about this clawback. When I questioned people, no one I spoke to was affected by this measure.
So I say, Let us stop this witch hunt, let us stop frightening seniors again. We are asking the most fortunate in our society to help us reach our goal of restoring our public finances, which we are striving for courageously.
December 19, 1989

I wanted to make this clarification, Madam Speaker, to help those following this debate see both sides and realize that we are not attacking universality of social programs, but asking the rich, from high-income individuals, to do more for the good of the public treasury.

Madam Speaker, I, too, rise to support the amendment brought forward by my colleague from Ottawa South.
Like so many other Canadians I am outraged that this government has unilaterally decided to send our tradition of universality of social programs down the slippery slope. I am speaking specifically of the clawback of which this Conservative government is so proud.
The arguments put forward for the clawback are superficially convincing. On the surface they appear to be rational, economically sound and even workable. However, much like the Communist system, the demise of which we have all been watching with great interest over the past month, in practice this theory, too, is unworkable because it is overlooks the element of the individual.
We are seeing today the demise of a system which appears on the surface to be grounded in principles of social equity and social justice. However, this system overlooks the human factor. Human beings are not complacent. They are ambitious and they have initiative. Totalitarianism overlooks these factors and subsequently is now beginning to collapse world-wide.
Thus we should learn from the examples around us and endeavour to make our own system more human, more open and more compassionate. Here in Canada the government uses similar non-human reasoning to justify the implementation of the clawback. They say the rich do not need it, why waste the money? Upper income pensioners and upper income parents should not receive social benefits, it is argued.
This is a strong persuasive argument on which the government bases its new policy. Let us analyse this argument to see how erroneous it actually is. The government claims that the clawback will only hit affluent families, but the truth of the matter is very different.
Government Orders
The truth of the matter is that a family with two children and one income in excess of $50,000 will pay back all its family allowances as a result of this policy. Such a family can hardly be called affluent by the rational person, but by this government it would be.
To complicate this scenario, what if this particular family lives in Toronto or Vancouver where the cost of living is astronomical? This family would still have to repay all of its family allowance.
Clearly, the threshold set by the government is too low. Even if we were to accept the argument, what would be a fair threshold, $60,000, $70,000, $100,000? The answer is simply none. There is no fair threshold because each family's specific circumstance is different. This government has shown that it is incapable of understanding the unique circumstances of any Canadian family.
Certainly, there will be those families which do not need the added benefits but the number of such families is marginal at best. In trying to create one standard which binds all families in a certain income category this government is running the danger of catching hundreds, if not thousands of others, in the same net who are deserving and in need of the benefits.
We find ourselves in a dilemma. Should we eliminate universality, save a few dollars and deprive many families of their deserved and needed benefits? Or should we be realistic and allow some families who do not particularly need the benefits to collect those benefits and ensure that all those families who need the benefits will receive them? Should we just tax back those benefits in the normal way rather than clawing them back in a way which is contrary to all the traditions of Canada and Canadian social programs? The answer for any reasonable and compassionate person is that we do not support the clawback.
I do not understand why this government is obsessed with destruction and devastation. It seems that at every turn the government wants to dismantle viable national institutions, our history, our infrastructure, the kinds of [DOT] things that have made us unique on the world stage as Canadians, the kinds of things that every member in this House in his or her secret soul is proud of, even our Minister of Finance, all in the name of deficit reduction. My colleague from Winnipeg St. James in a previous debate talked about canonizing the deficit reduction.

December 19, 1989
Government Orders
Well, it is canonized all right. It is canonized at the expense of individual Canadians.
The government is slashing social spending, dismantling VIA Rail, butchering UIC and now clawing back the benefits which families and seniors so desperately need.
What of old age pensions? Once again, members of the Conservative Party is going after our senior citizens. They tried it once before when they tried to deindex old age pensions and they were stopped in their tracks. The seniors of Canada would not have it then and they will not have it now. It is not bad enough that many seniors are unable to enjoy a decent standard of living as if that, in itself, was not one of the greatest black marks on the escutcheon of our country, this government is proposing to claw back old age pensions and run the danger of further impoverishing Canadian seniors.
Let us take the case of an elderly woman who lives off the interest from the proceeds of the sale of her family home. The interest may be enough to live comfortably. Yet because she is capital rich her old age pension will be clawed back, above and beyond the income tax she is paying on her interest income. We run the same danger with old age pensions as we run with family allowance benefits. That is, how can this government propose to create a scheme whereby only the few who truly do not need the benefits are exempt, again, without catching in the same net many others who need the benefits. It simply cannot be done.
Worse yet, worst of all is the abandonment of the traditional principles of universality which are based on the respect of the dignity of every individual Canadian. This abandonment will lead to a greater disparity between rich and poor. It will define lines of the needy and the not needy. It will ghettoize those families and seniors who receive the benefits particularly in the case of seniors, to the point where they will suffer even more because their pride will not allow them to seek such social programs as the guaranteed income supplement to help them get through. Why? Because if everyone does not get it, then as far as they are concerned it is a stigma to take it.
If we can do that to people who have spent their whole lives building this country, then we are not the heirs to the tradition of Canada that I hoped we were.
This brings me once again to the human factor of which I spoke earlier. Canadians are proud people, and rightly so. Canadians are also generous and tolerant. It is for this reason that we have believed in universal programs such as medicare.
We do not deny medical care benefits to someone who earns above a certain income. We do not deny these benefits because we believe that medical benefits should be available to everyone and there should not be a price placed upon an individual's health. The same principle applies uncategorically to family allowance and old age pension. There can be no price placed on the struggles of a family nor can there be any price placed on the dignity of our senior citizens, most of whom, if not all of whom, have contributed to this program.
In closing, universality is not, contrary to the opinion of this government, a dirty word. It is a proud word, it is a good word and, over and above all that, it is a Canadian word. Universality involves concepts of tolerance, fairness, equity and dignity. I have trouble understanding why this government finds such qualities so repugnant. I have trouble understanding why this government wants to tear down our values, our system and the things that we hold dear.
The time has come for this government to reassess its values. Canadians are tired of seeing the pillars of social equity being ripped down by a government obsessed with big business and international jet-setting.
I plead with the government to abandon its relentless attacks on seniors and families. If this government so enjoys crippling people, might I suggest it start directing its energy at foreign corporations and foreign fishing fleets and leave Canadian institutions, Canadian traditions and Canadian values alone.

Madam Speaker, perhaps I should lead off with the consultation paper of the present government from January of 1985 on child and elderly benefits, but I will save that for tomorrow. I am sure that hon. members will be very interested in that.
December 19, 1989

I should also make mention of the 125 government amendments to Bill C-28. Might I also quickly add that all these amendments have been ruled out of order. I suggest that all of these amendments will be tabled.
One has to ask why have the amendments been set aside. Someone has to suggest that the bill must be significantly flawed and, obviously, that the amendments are also flawed. If you put one piece of flawed legislation with 125 flawed amendments, obviously what you are going to come up with is a flawed bill.
In questioning the Minister of Finance about the amendments, he suggests, "No problem. These amendments are primarily technical in nature. These are going to be handled through the technical bill that we are putting into the House some time in the new year. But there are a couple of elements that are more pressing than that and they will be introduced through new legislation at an earlier date". I suggest that there is something dreadfully wrong with this piece of legislation.
I guess our track record is better. We have introduced nine amendments, six of which were at least accepted as being debatable, and for that we are grateful and very pleased. As to the 125 government amendments, are they consequential or inconsequential, we are not sure. That remains to be seen. We are certainly taking a serious look at them.
On behalf of the New Democratic Party, we support the amendment of my hon. friend from Ottawa South which suggests that the entire clawback provision be removed. We, too, introduced that kind of amendment and therefore, we have no difficulty in supporting it.
Nevertheless, reality sets in and we know that this majority government will ram this legislation through as it has done through first reading, second reading, committee stage and now at report stage and probably tomorrow-well, we know for sure tomorrow it will be all over. So this is the way the Tories have conducted themselves and we have to accept reality even though we do not like it. We understand what they are up to.
For your heart of hearts, we are providing you some honourable, noteworthy options which will win you favour with families and senior citizens across this country. This is favour that this government so sorely needs, especially taking into consideration the legislation
Government Orders
put forth this morning in the GST. The government needs to win some favour with Canadians, and particularly with seniors and families.
Amendment No. 6 would mitigate against the clawback provision. It would raise the threshold to $75,000 so fewer people would be affected now and even more important, fewer people would be affected in the future.
Amendment No. 7 is indexed to the Consumer Price Index. It is indexed to inflation. It is a splendid idea and not indexing seniors' pensions is what caused the government so many problems back in 1985. Surely it does not want to revisit that scene once again.
There is the sham of deficit reduction, the $300,000 or $500,000, whichever figure you want to believe. If you index it, you will still realize a certain amount of this figure. Yet you will indicate to all Canadians, not just seniors and young families, that you truly mean what you say, that for the most part universality will almost be preserved, is almost a sacred trust and at the very least please accept that.
In the budget papers of April 27, 1989, regarding the repayment of social transfers, the Minister of Finance said: "The level of threshold will be reviewed periodically and adjusted as appropriate." It begs the question: Is this going to be the same monitoring process that was in place for the free trade agreement? If so, we do not need that kind of monitoring process. Do away with it because there is none.
I understand the government now has hired an outside consultant to monitor the effects of the free trade agreement. We do not want to wait one year for the monitoring to start. Let us start monitoring immediately so we will save the government money, time, effort and the need to make further unpopular arbitrary decisions. Accept at least one of these amendments. It is the honourable option for the government to make its point yet realize some money while maintaining some semblance of credibility on this whole issue.
I see there are seven government members here. I would ask each of you to get out there and talk to 20-some of your fellow members and tell them of the good news, the good amendments that the New Democrats have brought forward. Tell them to support one of the amendments.

Government Orders
Government members told us in committee that we have to wrap this up before Christmas because it is a Christmas present. Here is a real opportunity to make seniors and families happy across this country. I urge the government to seize this opportunity.
We New Democrats have faith. We believe that one of our amendments will be accepted by the government, because it is the only honourable thing to do and we would be surprised and disappointed if the government did not support one of these amendments.
We all accept that it is very difficult for us to get the government to define what universality is. It keeps saying that if we give with one hand and take with the other, it is still universality. We reject that out of hand and we suggest that if it is affecting 4 per cent in 1991, it may affect 8 per cent in 2001 and 25 per cent in later years and so on.
When does universality cease to be universality? We say that universality is at an end today or tomorrow. It is at an end. It is a watershed of social policy that this country has become accustomed to and deserves. It is a right for all Canadians to enjoy.
If the government would save just a little bit of face at this Christmas time of the year and accept one of the amendments, you can buy the better of two worlds. Although not acceptable totally, at least it would buy you some credibility in your stated belief that universality and social programs are a sacred trust. We do not trust you and Canadians do not trust you. Here is a very small opportunity to save some face.

Madam Speaker, I rise to speak on the amendment to the clawback to the two great social programs that Canada has introduced. These two social programs, the family allowance and the old age security, are the envy of many nations of this world.
I would like to begin my remarks today by looking at the fiscal context in which these changes are being introduced. After all, the government has told Canadians that its primary problem is the deficit. Let us look at that.
The deficit in the five years this government has been in power has more than doubled. In spite of its Draconian cutting of programs and including cuts to these programs, the deficit this year is going to be even $1.6 billion higher than last year. This is on top of the most monumental tax increases that we have already seen which has amounted to 32 separate tax increases in five
years. Now what have they meant to ordinary Canadians?
Five years ago, income taxes paid in Canada were about $29 billion. This year, they are $80 billion, up 72 per cent in five years. What does this mean to an ordinary family? Well, in 1984, a family with two wage earners and two children with a combined family income of about $45,000 paid a fair share, and some could argue too much, income tax. But in the five years since 1984, that family's tax burden has increased by fully $2,800. When you add on to it the tax that was introduced in this House this morning, the goods and services tax, the increase to a $45,000 per year two-child family will be about $3,300.
Now, let us look at families at the poverty line. In five years, the taxes paid by families at the poverty level in Canada have increased fully 60 per cent. At the same time, the taxes paid by the rich in Canada have gone up only 8 per cent. If the problem were simply getting revenue, where should the government have gone for that revenue, to low and middle income families or to poverty level families in Canada? They went to the people who could afford it.
This is why we see today that fully 25 per cent of all Canadian children are living below the poverty level. This is a national disgrace for a country that has such wealth, even though our relative standard of living is declining vis-a-vis all our major trading partners.
Let us also look at some of the other reasons that we must reject the concept embodied in this Tory bill. The threshold at which the Tories claw back pensions and family allowances is $50,000, but that is not indexed. If inflation remains at the same rate as today, in about 10 years' time, fully one million Canadian families will have their pensions and old age security clawed back from them.
This government is saying: "You are the ones who are going to suffer". Inflation is not the fault of these taxpayers. It is the fault of these government policies. So why should the Tories impose the burden on Canadians who do not have it within their means to control the inflation rate?
This is a discriminatory tax on one-income against two-income families. Under these provisions, if you have two wage earners in a family who are earning $49,000 each, there is no clawback. There is no clawback on an income of almost $100,000. However, if you are a single-income family earning $50,000, the clawback

starts and it is fully complete when your income hits the $70,000 to $75,000 level. Is that fairness?
This is not a government which is prepared to even recognize that because of its Draconian tax policies and its high interest rate policies Canadian families now have to have more than one wage earner in order to just survive.
The government told us in the 1987 budget that when the new sales tax is introduced, the personal and corporate income surtaxes will be removed. We have just been told today, oh, no, the 3 per cent surtax on all incomes will stay in place. Not only that, it has increased to 5 per cent. This is another broken promise by a government that is not prepared to honour its election commitments.
We know now that it was prepared to do anything it could, prior to the election, to get elected, including holding off the introduction of its dreaded goods and services tax. The government did not have the guts to introduce it before the election. It waited until afterwards. Now the government is clawing back pensions and family allowances. Did the government tell us it was going to do that before the election? Absolutely not.
Why do you think Canadians become cynical? They become cynical when they are lied to, when they are cajoled and when they are treated in such an unfair and an inequitable way.
Let me conclude my remarks by saying that this bill has to be defeated because it is, in effect, a discriminatory tax on seniors. The government is saying to you: "If you are a senior citizen, then we will treat you differently from all other taxpayers. We are going to tax back a portion of your income. We are going to tax all of it back, and the reason we are doing that is simply because you are a senior citizen".
What does this say to Canadians who are saving for their future? These senior citizens can say: "I could have spent all my money and enjoyed my life. I need not have put aside money in order to provide for my security in old age. I could have spent it. I could have lived the good life, rather than being frugal and providing for my retirement. But, because I was frugal, my savings are going to mean that I am subject to this complete clawback. I am being jeopardized and discriminated
Government Orders
against, because I acted in a responsible way. I paid my taxes as I went along. I contributed to this pension".
These people never in their lives would have believed that they were going to be taxed back simply because they were senior citizens and simply because they no longer had the ability to go out and take an active part in the workforce.
Tories will tell you that they have increased the limit that you can contribute to pensions and to retirement savings plans. Bravo, but that only applies if you are an active member of the workforce, if you have the income and can go out and do it. Seniors cannot go back into the workforce to recoup the money that is being taxed back from them. This is why it is such an inequitable type of tax.
The Tories had alternatives in coping with the so-called deficit. They have chosen to do it on the backs of the impoverished, the low-income and the middle-income families. Canadians do not accept this, they never will. The government will find out at the next election how Canadians feel about these policies.

Madam Speaker, I am happy to have the opportunity to speak on Bill C-28 which is clawing back seniors' pensions. In my riding, there are over 20,000 senior citizens, and when I was campaigning in the last election, many seniors still had a memory of the attempt by the government to deindex their pensions in the Minister of Finance's first budget of 1984.
There was a fear, and I must tell you that that fear was not prompted. They still had a lingering memory about that attempt to deindex pensions. One of the things that we forget about senior citizens is that it is not that they do not want to pay their fair share, it is not that they do not want to continue to contribute to the fabric of this nation, but they are at a time in their lives when they feel that they have made a great contribution and they feel that they should be given a sense of security. When the government comes along and starts clawing back when there was absolutely no mention of this intent before the last election, they become very suspicious. They become

December 19, 1989
Government Orders
nervous. Some actually become almost terrorized, their feeling is so intense.
One of the things we overlook in this House is that very few people actually understand our tax system today. I know when I talk to the senior citizens in my riding, they say that they do not understand it any more. We have a tax system in this country that is so complicated, laid out in a document that has close to 15,000 or 16,000 pages, that even the best tax lawyers in the country will admit they cannot figure it out any more. If the best tax lawyers in the country are having a difficult time with it, how does this give a sense of security or a sense of trust to seniors?
Then we come along with a new system and we put out a memo saying that the $50,000 threshold at which individuals begin paying back their FA and their OAS benefits is only partially indexed to increases in inflation above 3 per cent, and this deindexing of the $50,000 threshold means that within 10 years, close to one million families will start losing their family allowances and old age pensions.
We know what this is all about because we spend time going over it and figuring it out. But, quite frankly, even after that I still have a difficult time understanding it. I think it is about time that we in this Chamber start to realize that our system is so complicated that it is acting as a disincentive, it is acting almost like a morale buster. When the morale of our community breaks down, it has a ripple effect. That is the problem we have with this government. It is breaking down the morale, it is breaking down the will of the country.
Seniors are a very effective communications force in this nation. We remember in 1984, when the seniors heard that their pensions were being indexed, from out of nowhere they were able to change the legislation of this government.
If the morale of senior citizens is not good, it affects the sons and daughters and those sons and daughters are entrepreneurs. They are teachers who, in turn, communicate to others. The whole spirit of this country can be affected.
I for one know of that communications ability of seniors and the effect they can have in a community because in my community, quite frankly, they got me elected. Their good word and positive attitude can affect
a lot of things. When the government targets seniors by clawing back pensions I think it is really being penny wise and pound foolish. The government is taking on the spirit of this country because senior citizens are the cornerstone of the spirit of this country.
We have heard many times in the last couple of weeks and months from the Minister of Finance saying: "Well, you are quick to criticize but what ideas do you have over there?" There are many of us who are working on ideas to try to come up with a more fair, more simple, more efficient and workable tax system and there is a group of us in my riding of Broadview-Greenwood. We have been working on this project called the single tax for many months. I stress that it is not our party policy at this time but it is an idea that we are discussing which will, hopefully, advance the debate in a constructive and a creative way.
I have talked to hundreds of seniors in my riding and they like this system because it is more simple, it is more fair. It is efficient. It will give the Government of Canada revenue neutrality. We do not need a goods and services tax with this system. We can phase out the manufacturers' sales tax over three and a half years. I can tell you that we used Statistics Canada models to run our numbers through on this. It will work.
I sent this package to the Minister of Finance. Of course, he has incredible resources. He has a Department of Finance with over 3,000 public servants who could take a look at this system, and I am prepared to accept his constructive criticism about the flaws in the position that I am putting forward. He should at least take a look at it and he should try to come back with what he thinks is wrong with it.
I have tested this in the market-place. We are getting good response. Many of my colleagues are finding the same thing. My point is that we have to start turning people on again in this country so that they are more enthusiastic about what they are doing. I am afraid that if we do not get excited about this country again in the next few months, we are going to slide into a recession. No one in this country wants that and we are not over here trying to criticize just for the sake of criticism, but it is our duty to criticize when a community like the senior citizens of Canada are being confronted by the Minister of Finance and his officials by a clawback system. These are people who have worked all their lives in anticipation

of their pensions. I mean, it is so small minded. I cannot understand it.
I am not saying that we should not pay attention to deficit or debt. We must. But there are better ways. It is incumbent upon all of us to take a look at the fact that we have been held captive by this 15,000 or 16,000 pages of "bureaucratese" for the last 20 years, and I think it is time that the people of Canada get a better deal. I can think of no better constituency than the senior citizens of Canada to begin the process of going back to basic comprehensive tax reform.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian L. Gardiner (Prince George -Bulkley Valley):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to participate in this debate on Bill C-28, legislation that has been very ably led on our side of the House by my colleague, the member for Sault Ste. Marie. Frankly, he has done a better job than the government.
As you know, at least a couple of his amendments were accepted by Your Honour, whereas 125 or 128 amendments proposed to this legislation at this particular stage were actually ruled out of order. I think a good deal of credit goes to my colleague for Sault Ste. Marie for the very competent work he has done and shame on the government for its incompetence in handling this legislation.
What is Bill C-28? Bill C-28 is an omnibus bill dealing with a number of matters. Today we are dealing with legislation on the clawback, as it has been referred to, but this legislation also does a number of other things. It has amendments to the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements Act respecting education and health. We have made comments on that. It deals with the Old Age Security Act, public utilities income tax transfer and the Income Tax Act as well as a host of others.
Our discussion at this stage of the bill, the report stage, where amendments are being presented by members in the House, is an important stage of debate. It is made more so because the closure party, the Conservative party, through a number of time allocation and closure measures that we spoke about yesterday gives rise to the headlines in the paper. Our very capable House leader, the member for Kamloops, talked about jackboot tactics. That is the way seniors are being treated in this country under Bill C-28.
Government Orders
I think it is a credit to the member for Sault Ste. Marie and our House leader that they have drawn the attention of Canadians to this legislation. It has been a bill run through the House by this government amidst grief and suffering taxes and a host of other items in the hope that it can get by with what is being called-and something that I can support-a wholesale and fundamental shift in the way that we will be dealing in the future with the questions of universality and social services.
I want to comment briefly on the question of universality. It is easy for the Prime Minister to get out and talk about how the opposition wants to help out the bank managers and wealthy Canadians, and to ask why we do not support his proposal on clawing back pensions from seniors.
Why? Why the defence of universality? The defence of universality goes around the reason why in this country we have built the kind of society that we have-hopefully, a sharing society and one where the benefits of all are not challenged by a few. What I mean by that is the reverse of universality is that the few, then, are not eligible. What does that mean? It goes back to the old days-before my time in this House, certainly-of means tests and other methods.
If we are trying to help all Canadians in society through broad tax measures and transfers of income, what we are talking about is having people line up for social assistance, for a means test or for any other kind of benefit. We are all going to be members of the United Way from now on because seniors are going to have to go to the United Way to get any kind of help, despite the time that they have spent building this country and getting us to the point where we have the resources and we have rights in this House, even though they are trampled on occasionally and, indeed, all too often now by the government. I would like to quote from a brief that was submitted to the legislative committee on Bill C-28 regarding the question of universality and the clawback as it has been referred to. I think it is an excellent summary of the debate that members on this side have been presenting to the government. It is my hope that in doing this some of the government members, in particular those members who I am sure have seniors in their riding, will pay attention and will vote on our side for some of the amendments that we are dealing with now.

December 19, 1989
Government Orders
Let me quote from the organization called One Voice, the Canadian seniors network. It was to the legislative committee on Bill C-28. The group was unable to appear because the government, of course, restricted the number of witnesses that could attend in order to try and get the bill through. I quote:
At a threshold of $50,000 the clawback has been put forward as a tax on the wealthy.
This has been accepted by most people because it has always been a pillar of Canadian taxation, that wealthy people should pay proportionately more in our progressive system. Fair enough. However, the threshold of $50,000 is only partially indexed. Over the years, that threshold will diminish until most average-income Canadians will be losing their benefits. Estimates show that partial indexation will reduce the threshold to $30,000 in less than 20years. It is also possible to foresee, once we have accepted the principle of the clawback, that a future federal budget, perhaps in March or April of next year, might arbitrarily lower the threshold to $40,000 or $30,000. At $30,000 the clawback is not a tax on the wealthy but a tax on all those in the middle and upper income categories. In fact, the government could have introduced the clawback at $30,000 at any level. But it chose not to. Why?
I think this is the answer to the debate about universality. The brief continues:
Because the clawback would then be seen not as a tax on the wealthy,-
This argument was presented by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance and a legion. There is not a legion of Tories here today, that is for sure. They do not want to hear the truth. The brief goes on:
-but for what it really is -recovery of benefits from part of the population.
This is an attack on the universality of Canada's social programs.
I would challenge the Conservative members of this House to put that description in their householder in the new year. I challenge them to run that description of this legislation. If the Conservative members ask their constituents and seniors in their riding to use the mailbacks to comment on Bill C-28 and the amendments that we have presented, you know very well what those constituents and those seniors will be doing to those Conservatives when the next election comes around. When is the jackboot going to hit the mark from the Conservatives, the jackboot that the Tories are laying on the seniors of this country.
This is to go into effect for tax year 1990. When Canadians are filing their tax returns in 1991-is that not a familiar sounding year-they will find other things happening. GST, grief and suffering tax, gouge and screw
tax, whatever you call it, seniors are going to be hit with this legislation which is an attack on the universality of social programs in Canada and an attack on average Canadians who are prepared to pay their fair share. I call on the government members to join with the opposition, support these amendments and defeat this regressive bill.

Madam Speaker, I regret very much the measure that is before the House now. Of course, I am rising with all members of the opposition to urge the government to think again about a change in our tax laws which hit so much at the fundamentals of what we understand Canada to be about. I am glad that the debate is taking place at a time when we are starting to see other news, news that I want to talk about in a moment. I hope this news is giving government members something to think about, whether the direction in which the Conservatives are leading Canada is really a direction in which they want to support the government. There are a number of government supporters in the House and I am glad to see them here. I hope that they will be considering these things as Christmas approaches, as news comes out more and more about the developing inequalities in Canadian society and about the power that we have in this House of Commons, as individual members representing the ridings and the regions of Canada, to stand up and do something about it.
When I was first elected, and in the two or three elections that followed, one of the most common questions that constituents would ask during election campaigns is no longer being asked. But in 1968, 1972, 1974 and 1978 one of the most common questions that you always got as you went around campaigning was, "What is the difference really between the Liberal and the Conservative parties anyway? What is the difference between what the two parties stand for in terms of leadership of the country?" That is not a question that Canadians ask at election time any more. They now have seen whatever it was that the Conservatives said in 1984 in order to get elected, whatever kind of make-believe Liberals-as one of our Senators put it in describing them-they appeared to be and seen the government demonstrate since coming to office a very different way of looking at Canada and of looking at how this country should be led.
December 19, 1989

The Conservatives believe in the trickle-down theory of economic benefit. They believe, and the Minister of Finance once said as much, "We need more rich people in Canada". The theory was that if we, as a society, could use the powers of government, use the taxation system to make the rich richer, to assist them in achieving their economic goals in society, that that would trickle down and it would eventually be good for the rest of Canadian society.
Liberals do not look at the country that way. We are happy to see people who are rich getting richer. We are happy to see ordinary Canadians achieving success and becoming better off because it means that they are making a contribution to the economy. But we, on this side of the House, recognize that just watching rich people get richer does nothing in itself to assure that ordinary Canadians, that poorer Canadians are going to become better off as a result.
When we look at some other countries in the world where there are very rich people, the theory that making the rich get richer is going to assure a trickle-down benefit to ordinary people in the society, we have a demonstration that that is not true. More and more we see in our country as we look around that although the rich may be getting richer, and more and more fortunes are being acquired and accumulated in Canada by economic effort that is beneficial to the economy and even creates jobs to a certain point, it is not a substitute for programs that look at the ordinary Canadian; that look at the poor; that look at regions of this country- which are becoming more and more desperate in spite of over-all national statistics to which the government points with pride-and that show that there is a missing ingredient, something missing in this government's planning that is moving us in a direction in which I think Canadians do not want to be led and in which I do not think Canadians will want to follow this government.
We have one illustration before us in the example of the clawback. I want to take some time to develop why we find the clawback so objectionable. But I cannot let this time of year pass without talking about the plight of children in Canadian society. We learned last week that there are more food banks in the city of Toronto now than there are McDonald's hamburger restaurants across our fair city. This is an appalling piece of informa-
Govemment Orders
tion for Canadians to absorb, for Torontonians to absorb: the idea that as we have seen our society becoming more prosperous as more businesses are becoming successful, even as there are more people in the city of Toronto working every month than there were in the last month, that because of the approach of this government which is being accompanied month by month by month with a greater and greater situation of poverty in the city of Toronto and in the country of Canada.
We have a social contract in this country that is being violated by this government. It is a social contract that better off Canadians understand very well. The contract is that we contribute, we work, we pay our taxes, we enjoy whatever benefits we earn in the Canadian society. We do so in the full belief, which is no longer true, but which has been true and which should be true that we as a society are caring for each other. When I take out my kids to celebrate a birthday and take all of our friends along to enjoy ourselves, the system which we have supported in the past is looking after the less fortunate in the society. It is hard for us to be responsible for the welfare of people in other countries far away from ours where we see so much suffering. It is not hard for us to be responsible for the welfare of our fellow Canadians. Far from setting an example in Canada of a caring society, we are being led by this government, with prosperity all around us, further and further away from that essential element of being Canadian which has made it such a wonderful country to live in, where we could enjoy our successes and our prosperity in those parts of society where we have earned it and where we have it, knowing that no one will be suffering, no Canadian children will be going to bed hungry at night when my own children are at birthday parties.
This is a very serious violation of the fundamental element of Canadianism. I urge members of the government party to consider this when they are voting on this cruel clawback measure to which I now want to turn my attention in the remaining few minutes that I have.
When I first started paying income tax, there was a little line on the form that said, "3 per cent old age security tax". I and millions of Canadians paid it. We understood by paying it that we when we became senior citizens-and I am a long way from it yet, but it is significant-we would receive an old age pension. The

most fraudulent feature of the presentation the government has made is its insistence that that commitment is being honoured even under the amendment that is being proposed today. Government members stand there with straight faces and tell Canadians, who contributed for years and years to their own old age security pension, that they have nothing to complain about and that they are still going to get it.
I hope there is no one in the country who believes this because Canadians will not be getting that pension. As we who are still far from retirement get closer and closer to it, the proportion of the old age pension to which we have contributed and which was part of that fundamental, social contract of Canada, is being clawed back by a tax system which is probably unconstitutional and which, although it does not violate a specific contract that we had when we paid that 3 per cent, does violate the spirit of universality, which is one of the essential components of being Canadian.
For those whose income is between $25,000 and $50,000, a greater and greater proportion of the money received every year as the old age pension will be clawed back at double tax rates so that when you reach $50,000, the whole of that old age pension that the government says you are still getting is going to be completely reimbursable to the Government of Canada.
A $50,000 a year retiree is certainly not a pauper, neither is a $25,000 a year retiree, but that is not the point. The point is that this payment was part of the commitment made to working Canadians while they were contributing to the tax. I used to work in the field of pension taxation and pension law. I know that there are hundreds of pension plans across this country which are specifically reduced by the amount of the old age pension that the retiree is going to receive.
Under most of these plans, unless they are revised, and I do not think they will be, this insidious clawback provision will not alter the amount payable to the retiree so that, for purposes of the private plan to which you contributed, your pension will be reduced as if you were getting an old age pension, but when you make out your tax return every year and when you send it in you will find that you are getting less than you agreed to receive
when you contracted your particular retirement plan as one of the negotiated conditions of your employment.
It is a fraud to tell Canadians that they are getting the old age pension and to have their plans set up on that basis when they are clawed back eventually to the level of zero.
I see that the 10 minutes I have has expired, but I want to add one other idea. With inflation, which is almost guaranteed even at very low levels year after year after year, that $25,000 cut-in and that $50,000 threshold get closer and closer and closer to the poverty level of an individual. What this means is that while this year you can look at a $25,000 a year retiree or a $50,000 a year retiree as being better off, that will not be the case when people my age are ready to retire and when all the other people who have sent us here to Parliament on their behalf will retire.
I urge government members to think about what we are doing in the opposition to resist this insidious, un-Canadian amendment to the Income Thx Act.

Mr. Speaker, the Free Trade Agreement with the United States enables Canadian industry to compete with the Americans. The gradual elimination of customs tariffs on Canadian goods exported to the United States has

made it possible for one business in my riding to break into the U.S. market and thus become established on the international market.
Elenri Fontaine Limitee in Magog, a well-known family business, has just signed a major contract worth $1.5 million with California to manufacture 200 wall-mounted valves made of stainless steel, to be used in waste water treatment.
Its competitors, Mr. Speaker, were major U.S. companies well known in the field. This is indeed a feather in the cap of Fontaine Limitee which is celebrating its 25th anniversary this year.
For these two reasons I offer my sincere congratulations to the firm's president and its employees.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as part of the cruel and unusual punishment inflicted upon the residents of the national capital area the government has announced the closure of the production facility of the Canadian Government Exposition Centre. This decision will result in the layoff of some 50 workers just a few days before Christmas.
Perhaps even more serious, if anything could be more serious and more devastating than learning that you are losing your job just a few days before Christmas, this decision made by the government does not make any sense using the government's own criteria.
At a time when we are incurring a trade deficit in this country, the Canadian Government Exposition Centre is very much needed. This kind of facility prepares exhibits and displays for the Government of Canada when travelling throughout this country and the whole world. Indeed, if we did not have a Canadian Government Exposition Centre this would probably be the most opportune time to create one in order to increase trade opportunities for our country.
Shame on the government.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance this morning said that the government is responding to small business concerns over the GST. How wrong he is. Small business had been offered a $600-a-year fee to collect the GST. That has been taken away. Small business had been promised that it would be consulted to find further ways of streamlining the tax. The Canadian Federation of Independent Business has called the streamlining "easily the most complex part of the GST proposals".
Small business exemptions on new cash register equipment will total only 20 per cent of the cost. In my own riding of Surrey North I am receiving letters from small businesses protesting the added expense of the GST.
In addition, they point out that the required paperwork will also reveal to everyone both the costs and profits of any small business. No wonder small business has completely rejected the GST. No wonder John Bulloch of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business calls the GST "a triumph of greed and politics over reason and sound tax planning".

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to pay tribute to volunteer agencies which serve the less fortunate in our country at this time of year. There are church groups, service clubs, scouts, girl guides and many other organizations that attempt to bring the spirit of Christmas to those in need.
I pay special tribute to the Salvation Army which will be providing shelter, clothing, food hampers and Christmas dinners for over 80,000 people across Canada alone. As a physician I note the tremendous efforts of the Salvation Army and its officers to fight chemical dependency involving not only hard drugs but also alcohol and tobacco which are causing severe health and social problems today. Emotional, material and spiritual support provided to the poor is doing much to combat problems of child poverty.

December 19, 1989
I appeal to all Canadians to share our abundance with the army and to reach out to someone in need at this time of year when poverty is darker, hunger is deeper and loneliness is greater. Let us do our part to assist in bringing the true spirit of love, joy, peace and goodwill to our fellow men at this special Christmas season.

Mr. Speaker, last Friday the Government of Canada and the province of New Brunswick signed a five year $91 million co-operation agreement on forestry development. The federal government will be contributing $50 million, the provincial government $41 million.
This agreement has been eagerly anticipated by New Brunswick's forestry sector and will make a significant contribution to the economy of the province as well as ensuring that the resource is wisely managed and protected for future generations.
I commend the federal and provincial governments for concluding an agreement that is so vital to the well-being of New Brunswick.

Mr. Speaker, Canada risks losing the services of the John Howard Society. The John Howard Society is concerned about new security conditions imposed on it by the Correctional Services of Canada. Correctional Services has imposed additional security conditions on voluntary organizations which provide prison visitation programs, operate halfway houses and conduct community assessment, parole supervision and other corrections programs.
The autonomy of private agencies is threatened and the privacy of individual employees is endangered. The new rules remove the right of independent agencies to determine whether employees are trustworthy and reliable in maintaining the confidentiality of information. The John Howard Society says that these new provisions are unnecessary in light of the organization's past success in ensuring security and confidentiality.
As a result of the changes, the society will become nothing more than an underpaid arm of government, void of local accountability and autonomy. After more than 30 years of providing parole supervision, Canada risks losing the services of the John Howard Society. I ask that the government rethink this policy in light of the contribution made by this organization to all of the country.

Mr. Speaker, at last TV viewers in some parts of the province of Quebec will receive the signal of CBC Newsworld. This is great news for national unity. In these difficult times for our country, I urge every member of Parliament to support my proposal to open CBC Newsworld to all regions of Quebec. In my view it is unacceptable that my constituents be blacked out by TV cable companies from a national service.
Yesterday, a French-speaking TV critic, Daniel Rioux, from le Journal de Montreal stated that CBC Newsworld will help Quebecers to better understand the reality of other Canadians.
I also want to remind this House that the CRTC rejects such a national service in French. It is about time that members of Parliament express themselves on this very important topic.

Mr. Speaker, today's announcement of a 7 per cent goods and services tax by the Minister of Finance will have a devastating effect on the more than 100,000 Canadians employed directly and indirectly in the horsebreeding and racing industry. These jobs will be decimated when the goods and services tax is implemented.
According to the chairman of the Ontario Racing Commission, higher costs and lower profits resulting from the GST would drive what remained of Canada's lucrative horse racing business to the United States.
In my riding of Hillsborough, the Charlottetown Driving Park paid approximately $813,000 in provincial taxes last year. If the GST is levied on the horse breeding and racing industry, whether at 7 per cent or 9 per cent, the
December 19, 1989

industry will not be able to absorb this additional cost. The loss of jobs and eventually the demise of the industry will be the result.
The government has not listened to the industry officials. Today the minister tried yet another smokescreen, the elimination of the existing .8 per cent federal agricultural levy on pari mutuel betting. Removing this levy while still implementing the GST will in no way lessen the damage suffered by the industry.
I strongly urge this government to withdraw the GST and go back to the drawing board.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 6, some 43 days ago, the duly elected members of this House passed the unemployment insurance bill, Bill C-21, a bill which would strengthen the ability of the UI program to act as an effective economic safety net, allow for more skills training and help Canadian workers better adjust to change.
Since that time, however, a group of non-elected Liberal senators have once again got caught up in another attempt to thwart the efforts of this government, look for loopholes in the rules and intentionally delay the legislation and demonstrate their political muscle.
Yet, where do the interests of the unemployed in Canada's poorer regions fit in? A distant second, it would seem. For these individuals the extra four week requirement could prove to be devastating, especially in light of the combination of other problems which they face.
I call upon all Liberal members opposite to urge their Senate colleagues to get on with it, to pass this much needed legislation and start putting the needs of Canadians in our poorer regions before this unnecessary self-interest and political showmanship.

Mr. Speaker, I would have liked to have put a cheerful face on my statement in keeping with this joyful season. But, as members of Parliament head home to feast, I ask them to consider images of starving children in the Third
World and developing countries lining up to receive life-saving food that Canada has sent. And we feel satisfied with our generosity.
Consider that close to one million Canadian children live in poverty. In this season of giving Canadians give to the hundreds of food banks across Canada to help these kids have a decent meal during the holidays. And we feel satisfied with our generosity.
I ask hon. members in this House to consider the other 364 days a year that these one million Canadian kids go to school and play while hungry. We cannot be satisfied with our generosity while one child is hungry and living in poverty. Consider this Christmas, as we give thanks for our good fortune, ways in which we can work together in this House toward eradicating poverty in 1990.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister of Canada asked in the House that the Senate pass Bill C-21 on unemployment insurance reform as quickly as possible, and he condemned the obstructionist tactics of the Liberal senators who have a majority in the other place.
This bill will make it possible to allocate $800 million to manpower training programs. It increases the number of weeks of employment required to be eligible for benefits and also reduces the number of benefit weeks. The CNTU approves provisions that increase maternity benefits and benefits for workers aged 65 and over.
Mr. Speaker, once again, the uncalled for obstruction by certain Liberal senators in the other place is totally unacceptable.

Mr. Speaker, daily we hear of dramatic changes in central and east European countries which bring new freedom, hope for justice and peace to the region. However, Romania remains intransigent in its Fascist repression of its people under the leadership of the dictator, President Ceauses-cu. We are all alarmed at the present news of the violence in Timisoara, Romania, reminiscent, in fact, of

December 19, 1989
the Tiananmen Square massacre in China earlier this year.
In Canada we have watched the increased persecution of the two million Hungarian minority in Romania and its protestant leader, the Reverend Laszlo Tokes. We wrote letters. We have watched Romanian masses being subjected to cold, hunger and misery, only to reward a dictator's blind, inhumane obsessions to pay off foreign debt.
Despite this, we have continued to trade with Romania. In recognition of Romania as a country where there is no freedom of expression, religion, association, and assembly, where the government massacres its own people, where we know there is no human rights commitment, Canada must act. Canada must press Gorbachev to intervene with compassion in the situation in Romania. We must reassess our trade with Romania. We must guarantee that Romania abides by the non-proliferation provisions of our Candu reactor trade contract. We must commit to bold action, not just the use of words.

Mr. Speaker, last October, after six months of thorough debate and coast-to-coast public hearings, this House passed Bill C-21 which will inaugurate significant improvements to Canada's UI system.
Atlantic Canadians need the additional access to employment and training opportunities which Bill C-21 will bring into effect. Atlantic Canadians approve of tightening up the system so there are less abuses of it. Atlantic Canadians need the benefit of variable entrance requirements.
I am really appalled at the utter contempt which the Liberal party, through its use of the other place, shows for democracy in this country. I say to the Leader of the Opposition, end the hypocrisy that purports to show an interest in unemployed Canadians while in fact doing them in. Let democracy prevail. End the MacEachen blackmail.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to bring to the attention of the House the issue of the MX Rail Garrison Program.
On November 29 the American air force announced its finalized plans for modernization of its nuclear missile force in North Dakota. Four trains, each armed with two MX missiles, will be stationed in Grand Forks. Each MX missile has 10 accurate, independently targeted and extremely powerful warheads.
The trains allow for mobility of the MX in times of crisis, making them less targetable than standard ICBMs and creating uncertainty for the so-called enemy. They have a destabilizing effect and represent a serious escalation in the arms race.
The stationing of MX-equipped rail cars so close to the Canadian border, not only in North Dakota but at several other American bases, should be protested by the Canadian government. It represents an unwelcome addition to the already considerable nuclear arsenal. There are presently 1,500 warheads in North Dakota alone, only miles from Canadian territory.
I urge the government to speak out against this inappropriate escalation of the arms race and, failing removal of the MX rail cars, to seek a guarantee that these trains will never move in the direction of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to express my disappointment with the behaviour and activities of the minister responsible for the Cape Breton Development Corporation. Union representatives and management personnel are in the midst of negotiating a collective agreement.
The minister has intervened by placing on the table the possible closure of the Lingan colliery which employs 1,200 persons. He has threatened that if a collective agreement is not signed for a duration of four years this

particular mine will close, affecting that community not only in the short term but, indeed, in the long term.
I would have hoped that the minister responsible would have wanted to facilitate the collective bargaining process. In that regard I ask him to call upon the Minister of Labour to appoint Bill Kelly, former Deputy Minister of Labour, as the mediator in this particular settlement in order to have this matter resolved before we break for Christmas. I urge the minister to do this forthwith.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I am sure the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition would want to put his question.

Mr. Speaker, small businesses in this country have opposed this sales tax right from the outset. For daring to stand up to the Minister of Finance the small business community received another kick in the teeth this morning. In order to teach the small business community a lesson, the minister gave them a $600 million kick in the teeth by taking away the fee that they were supposed to receive for administering his tax.
The minister told hardworking, decent, independent Canadian business people that they would receive an administrative fee for administering the nightmare that this tax is going to bring. Today he broke that promise.
What explanation is he going to give to the million small business people in this country for having once again broken his word, or does he think that the changes he announced this morning will relieve small business of that administrative nightmare?

Mr. Speaker, first of all let me make it quite clear that if the Leader of the Opposition had spent some time trying to understand this tax he would know that it is not an administrative nightmare. There have been a number of proposals that have been specifically brought in to the GST proposal, including two forms of streamlined accounting. If others are brought to our attention that are workable, we will allow those to be used as well.
We have also provided the small business community a relief from sales tax on the purchase of new equipment that they might need for compliance with the sales tax, that is point of sale equipment as well as inventory control equipment. That will drop the cost of that by about 20 per cent, which is not insignificant.
The final point I have to make is that the small business community, particularly led by the Chamber of Commerce, has been one of the loudest proponents of a lower sales tax rate. That is what we have brought in as a
result of my proposal this morning. The drop from 9 per cent to 7 per cent is a major step forward in meeting the concerns of the small business community.

Mr. Speaker, a few months ago the Minister of Finance recognized the administrative difficulty that small business would have by allowing them a fee to administer the tax. Every small business representative who appeared before the committee chaired by the member for Mississauga South told the committee, and through the committee told Parliament, that the tax would be an administrative nightmare: two sets of taxes, one federal, one provincial, two sets of books. Absolutely impossible for the average small business person to administer.
This morning the minister admitted for the first time that there was a slowdown in the economy. He said that the economy was slowing down. Yet at this dangerous time the minister insists on proceeding with this inflationary tax. At a dangerous time for the economy he is imposing a new goods and services tax upon Canadians.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
On Friday, November 3, the hon. member from York Centre sought to obtain the unanimous consent of the House in order to raise a question of privilege at the outset of the sitting without having submitted written notice.

The substance of the question had to do with what the hon. member for York Centre characterized as the deliberate interference by an official of the Federal Business Development Bank with the delivery of documents which the Bank had agreed to provide. He indicated that he wanted these documents in order to turn them over to the RCMP. In anticipation of their receipt, he had arranged a meeting with RCMP people in his office on the Thursday afternoon. As it happened, the documents were not turned over to the hon. member for this meeting.

The hon. member from Glengarry-Prescott-Russell supported the question of privilege and explained that the material requested from the bank was in the public domaine, as these documents had already been given to The Montreal Gazette. He went on to state that the failure of the bank to deliver the documents in the time previously arranged prevented the hon. member from York Centre from turning them over to the RCMP. Both members asserted that the decision to withhold the documents by an Ottawa official of the bank interfered
December 19, 1989

with the rights and obligations of that member to fulfil his responsibilities as a member of Parliament.

At the same time, however, the hon. member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell explained that the Federal Business Development Bank subsequently agreed to release the documents.
It would therefore appear that the question of privilege relates to a delay in the delivery of documents to the hon. member for York Centre which prevented him from keeping his appointment with the RCMP as originally planned. While the member may have been inconvenienced, it is difficult for the Chair to be convinced that this constitutes a question of privilege.

While there was a delay, it does not seem to be clear that the hon. member was hindered in the performance of his duties. Inconvenienced perhaps, but not interfered with.
I might also add that even though it was claimed that the documents were in the public domaine, it appears to me that, in fact, these documents remained the property of the bank. If by virtue of an internal decision or mix-up, and I do not want to suggest motives, the documents were not delivered when the member from York Centre had expected them, it seems to me that it is a matter to be resolved between the member and the bank.
As it happens, the bank has agreed to release the documents and that agreement was evidently made before this question of privilege was raised here. The matter, therefore, would appear to be resolved.
I thank the hon. member for bringing the matter to the attention of the House.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Resuming debate. The hon. member for Mount Royal.

Madam Speaker, I rise to speak to Motion No. 4 and Motion No. 7, on Bill C-28, but do sincerely regret that we are under a time allocation threat in this House. It is one that is used constantly and I think shows disrespect for the democratic process that would reflect our ability to speak to this issue in the name of all of our constituents.
This debate really symbolizes the Conservative party's true agenda. The issues we are discussing include the clawbacks of seniors pensions and family allowance. They are fundamentally an erosion of the universality principle that has always guided the social programs in this country.
The Conservative agenda appears aimed at cutting and reducing that caring aspect of government while saying that it is "in the national interest".
Well, I do not think that we agree. This is where we part company because we believe in a far more balanced approach and a much more fiscally responsible approach, always respecting a more compassionate tradition upon which our country was founded.
Throughout Canada's history, with all the change that has been wrought over its 120 years, there has always remained this one deeply held fundamental principle. That conviction has been a cornerstone of our national life and has not changed for many decades. It is our tradition of universal access to social programs, whether they be our medicare programs, our unemployment insurance programs, family allowance, Old Age Security and where needed, guaranteed income supplements, veterans allowances, et cetera. It was Canada's way of being fair and tolerant as a society.
Yet in 1984 that tradition had begun to unravel. It is this unravelling that I would like to talk about today. Since coming into office the Conservatives have time after time, year after year, continued a slow and very deceptive but always real plan to dismantle the safety net

Government Orders
of social programs that most of us believe were part of the fabric of this country.
It used to be everyone's right as a Canadian to have equal access to social programs. That is no longer true. That contract has been broken. Universality is such a simple idea, really. It is so easy to understand. It is the expression of a belief that over a lifetime every Canadian contributes to the building and flourishing of this society in their own way, and to the best of their ability, and that no one should be shut out from the benefits of the country that they have helped to build. That is universality.
In most instances its benefits are taxable in the hands of the receiver based on income levels. That is a fair and universal approach. The member thinks that is what they have done but it is not so.
We must remember that universality survived governments of both political parties, survived recessions and, indeed, grew out of the depression. Yet this spirit and tradition of a government looking out for the health and welfare of every Canadian, no matter where they live, no matter what their means, has come to a sudden end with this government since 1984.
Universality has become little more than words on a paper, words offered to Canadians on the one hand, then quickly erased with the other. How familiar we are with the Prime Minister standing before a crowd and declaring to all the country that our social programs were a sacred trust. Yes, there were days when this government's smooth rhetoric tricked Canadians into believing it shared this caring approach to social programs.
But it seems to have been a mask behind which has lain the real truth. Time after time this government has used fast talk and colourful packaging to hide from Canadians the true facts of the slow and determined dismantling of universal access to social programs and, in particular, the old age security for which these people have already paid. They started paying in 1952 and to this day they have been paying. But this government does not care to acknowledge this.
If it was a private sector pension plan, this government would not have allowed this kind of action for one second, but because it is the public sector it feels it can
just go about doing this without consulting the public and to the detriment of everyone in this country.
In five long years of opposition we have been devoting endless energy trying to stop this government's slow piece by piece erosion of social benefits.
It was early in their mandate that the unravelling really took place. I go back to December 21, 1984, just weeks after the Conservatives took office, when the finance minister first proposed the de-indexing of old age pensions. We know what happened. We know what Madam Solange Denis said and we knew that Pinocchio's nose was getting longer and longer.
Liberals began to battle with this government because they could not seem to understand why we were so committed to universality. It is because Canadians believed in fairness and in equality.
Oh, oh!
